The content of this document is proposed to be made by the Minister of Education as
a National Curriculum Statement under section 90(1)(a) of the Education and Training
Act 2020. Once made and published in the New Zealand Gazette, it will set the
requirements for the teaching of Years 0-10 Science in state schools, and schools will
be required to start using it from 1 January 2027.
Depending on their contexts, some schools may not be ready for full implementation
on day one of the 2027 school year, so the following transition arrangements are
proposed to apply:
•   For students in Years 0-8, schools will need to make a start by developing, and
    then executing, a plan that achieves full implementation as soon as practicable
    and by no later than the end of 2028.
•   For students in Years 9-10, schools will need to make a start by developing, and
    then executing, a plan that achieves full implementation as soon as practicable
    and by no later than the end of 2027.
Implementation requirements for specified kura boards will be confirmed when the
proposed National Curriculum Statements are made under the Act and published in
the New Zealand Gazette. This is to allow more time for the Crown to engage with
Kaupapa Māori education providers through their representative bodies in advance of
these proposed decisions affecting their kura. A specified kura board means the
board of any of the following:
•   a kura kaupapa Māori
•   a designated character school with a character that is hapū- or iwi-based or that
    affiliates with Ngā Kura ā-Iwi o Aotearoa
•   a state integrated school with a special character that is hapū- or iwi-based.

      statement
                                                By great thought the house is built; by knowledge it is made firm.




Science is the systematic, dynamic, and evidence-based discipline that builds and
organises knowledge through observation, prediction, testing, and analysis of the
world around us.

Science fosters students’ curiosity and helps them make sense of their everyday
experiences and the environments in which they live.
Science provides students with practical skills and ways of thinking that can be used
in a wide range of situations. As they progress, they apply disciplinary knowledge and
scientific practices together to explain observable phenomena and solve problems in
familiar contexts. Students understand how people, ecosystems, and resources are
connected. They learn to use scientific knowledge to help them make informed
decisions, think critically, and engage with scientific issues that affect people,
communities, and the world.

The Science learning area prepares students with the knowledge and practices to
access related curriculum subjects for Years 11–13.

 Observing relies on systematic observation using the five senses and scientific
  instrumentation, such as microscopes, to examine objects and events. Success in
  this method relies on accurate recording, often through labelled diagrams or tally
  charts.
 Classifying and identifying is the process of organising objects or events into logical
  categories based on their specific features. By utilising identification keys and
  naming systems, scientists can better understand the structural relationships within
  the natural world.
 Pattern seeking is used to identify correlations and trends within data, particularly in
  natural environments where variables cannot be strictly controlled. The collection of
  numerical measurements or counts across a broad range of data points is required
  to ensure the reliability of conclusions.
 Fair testing is a rigorous experimental design used to isolate and examine the
  causal relationship between specific variables. A strict protocol must be followed to
  maintain the integrity of the investigation:
  o Independent Variable: Only one factor is intentionally changed.
  o Dependent Variable: One factor is measured to determine the result.
  o Controlled Variables: All other factors are kept constant to ensure the results are
    valid and the cause of the effect is clearly identified.

                                                                                        thermoregulation.
                                                                                       Temperature receptors in the skin and the brain detect changes
                                                                                        in body temperature.
                                                                                       The brain coordinates responses through the nervous system
                                                                                        to maintain a stable internal body temperature.
                                                                                       Sweating and vasodilation decrease body temperature by
                                                                                        increasing thermal energy loss.
                                                                                       Shivering and vasoconstriction increase body temperature by
                                                                                        reducing thermal energy loss and generating thermal energy.
                                                                                       Thermoregulation maintains body temperature within a narrow
                                                                                        range and is an example of homeostasis.
